## About

I turn fragmented codebases into standards other teams build on.

I have full professional working proficiency in Chinese (DLPT5 3/3), Finnish at B1 and Swedish at A1. That global perspective translates into frontend work that spans cultures: internationalization, timezone-aware interfaces, and datetime handling that works across regions and calendar systems.

## Raising the bar

Technical leadership without formal authority. Reach scale, low to high:
My code → My team → Other teams → The whole platform → Outside the company.

### Temporal standard
**Reach:** Outside the company (Became public as @northguild/gmt)

Timezone bugs were a recurring class across the platform, not isolated incidents: each fix was a patch, and the patches produced the next bug. I set a Temporal-first standard for date and time handling, built as an internal package every application could depend on, a modeling decision I made and owned without waiting for sign-off.

“The engineering work was the smaller half. The larger half was making the architectural case to people who hadn’t been in the weeds of those bugs, then getting other teams to actually adopt it.”

100% data integrity on global bookings, and the bug class stopped recurring.

- Removed: each timezone bug fixed where it surfaced
- Added: one Temporal-first standard, as an internal package
- Added: every application on the platform depends on it
- Added: shipped publicly as @northguild/gmt # 61,613 tests across 10 time zones
- Added: bugs reported upstream to the polyfill and TC39 proposal # 11 issues and PRs

### Component & utility libraries
**Reach:** The whole platform (Five shipped products on one platform)

At Corivo I owned the architecture of the internal component and utility standardization used across the platform’s applications.

- Added: shared utility libraries
- Added: a UI component package
- Added: cross-app theming
- Added: a PDF generation service # across five shipped products

### Design tokens
**Reach:** The whole platform (The whole Micetro platform)

At Men&Mice I led the design-token standardization effort, working directly with the design team, and unified legacy components into a WCAG-compliant design system.

- Removed: legacy components
- Added: Figma libraries and plugins # with the design team

- Added: one WCAG-compliant design system

## Open source

Published npm packages and projects under @northguild, the GitHub collective I co-maintain with a former Travel Connect colleague.

### NorthGuild
https://northguild.dev/

The home page of @northguild: open-source tools for developers, built in the frigid north. Links to gmt and worktree, set over night-sky panoramas of Ísafjörður and Helsinki where the stars, moon, mountains and skyline are real and only the aurora is simulated.

### gmt
https://northguild.dev/gmt/

“Give Me Temporal!”: a TypeScript library wrapping the Temporal API in strings-in, strict-types-out helpers to kill Date bugs. 659 functions backed by 61,613 tests across 10 time zones and 3 Node versions, checked weekly against Chromium’s native Temporal. Ships with companion lint packages for oxlint, ESLint and Biome, and a docs site with a WebGPU time zone globe and Dox, an AI documentation assistant. Published as @northguild/gmt, v1.19.0, 1,097 npm downloads in the last 30 days.

### worktree
https://northguild.github.io/worktree/docs

A CLI for the daily Git worktree flow: create, copy .env, open the editor, clean up. Includes an embedded “Chat with the Docs” AI assistant.

### run-cv
https://github.com/northguild/run-cv

A mainframe-inspired terminal CV viewer built with Node, React and Ink. Try with `npx run-cv craig`.

### CodeVault
https://accesscodevault.vercel.app/

A developer knowledgebase SaaS built on Next.js, Neon Postgres, Prisma, Upstash Redis and Stripe.

### Mission Control
https://craig-o-curtis.github.io/mission-control/

A flexible database POC paying homage to Star Trek: The Next Generation. Built with Python FastAPI and SvelteKit on Svelte 5, served on Render, connected to SQLite and Postgres databases.

### Reporting bugs in JavaScript’s date standard, upstream

While hardening gmt against the TC39 Temporal specification, I found real bugs in the official Temporal polyfill and in the proposal’s own reference implementation, and reported them to both, as verified issues and proposed fixes. gmt already gives the correct answer for every one of them.

Live status: https://northguild.dev/gmt/upstream

#### js-temporal/temporal-polyfill
https://github.com/js-temporal/temporal-polyfill

The community polyfill every library runs on until Temporal ships natively.

- PR #367 (Range limits): A UTC shortcut skipped a range check, so a result past the last representable instant returned instead of failing. https://github.com/js-temporal/temporal-polyfill/pull/367
- PR #368 (Calendars): The Japanese calendar gave the wrong era for 1868–1872. https://github.com/js-temporal/temporal-polyfill/pull/368
- PR #369 (Calendars): Non-Gregorian dates near the ends of the supported range crashed. https://github.com/js-temporal/temporal-polyfill/pull/369
- PR #370 (Calendars): Counting months in Hebrew or Persian dates near the range limits threw. https://github.com/js-temporal/temporal-polyfill/pull/370
- PR #371 (Time zones): A transition in the last weeks before the maximum date was missed, crashing startOfDay and hoursInDay. https://github.com/js-temporal/temporal-polyfill/pull/371
- PR #372 (Time zones): The transition search started in 1847, missing Manila’s 1844 date-line crossing: hoursInDay returned 479,340 hours for a 24-hour day. https://github.com/js-temporal/temporal-polyfill/pull/372
- Issue #373 (Release): Release request: fixes already on main hadn’t reached users, and a release would also close #341 and #347. https://github.com/js-temporal/temporal-polyfill/issues/373

#### tc39/proposal-temporal
https://github.com/tc39/proposal-temporal

The standard’s own repository, home of the reference implementation.

- Issue #3327 (Calendars): A recent change made non-Gregorian month counting wrong at ordinary dates, and throw near the range limits. https://github.com/tc39/proposal-temporal/issues/3327
- Issue #3328 (Time zones): The time zone search bug before the maximum date, reported where the reference code lives, with the same fix. https://github.com/tc39/proposal-temporal/issues/3328
- Issue #3329 (Calendars): An assertion assumed unreachable can be reached, in the Coptic and Ethiopian calendars’ short 13th month. https://github.com/tc39/proposal-temporal/issues/3329
- Issue #3330 (Time zones): The 1844 date-line search bug, reported where the reference code lives, with the same fix. https://github.com/tc39/proposal-temporal/issues/3330

Verified by:
- Expected values from the spec text, test262 and Chrome’s native Temporal, never from the polyfill
- Every patch run on a production build of the polyfill’s main branch, with and without the change
- The 1844 fix checked across all 418 time zones: 1,672 rows against Chrome, 6,336 transition lookups byte-identical
- The project’s own jest and test262 suites, reported on each pull request

Not waiting on upstream:
- A probe checks once whether the installed polyfill still has each bug; if not, the workaround never runs
- A canary (pnpm compat) reports which workarounds a new polyfill release makes removable
- 409,552 calendar comparisons against Chrome’s native Temporal, 0 mismatches

## Agents

I run agents as a pipeline, not a chat window. Each story gets its own git worktree from a CLI I wrote. A planner grills me on every open decision and writes a handoff, but no code. A driver builds from that handoff through role-specific subagents, including a test-first developer that writes the failing test before the code, then sends every story through three reviewers: QA, security and accessibility. A reviewer may prove a finding with a failing test but never fixes it. Agent behaviour is written once, in AGENTS.md and one manifest per agent, and every harness I use reads it through a thin stub: Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code chat on local models.

Git belongs to me. Builders and reviewers never commit. One finalizer runs every check, walks the definition of done and cuts commits a reviewer can read one at a time, and it asks me before every push. Releases publish from CI with npm trusted publishing and provenance, and only when I merge a release PR. Lint, typecheck, tests and build are the definition of done for me and for agents; CI runs them on every PR and fails when published numbers or the story tracker drift from source. Nothing ships that I haven’t read.

### The crew

- **planner** — Finds the gaps in a story and grills me in rounds, then writes the handoff. Starts in plan mode. Writes no code: only the handoff, and spec edits I approve.
- **driver** — Runs a story from handoff to PR: tasks to builders, every story to three reviewers. Never re-plans, never writes app code, never commits.
- **api-maker** — Builds from the database to the page: API, migrations, shared types, server code. Test first, and only the task and files the driver names.
- **tdd-dev** — Builds pages and components: a failing test first, then the code. Never touches a database. If the route it needs doesn’t exist, it stops and reports.
- **3d-animator** — Owns all motion: transitions, springs, view transitions, later 3D. Every motion gets a reduced-motion branch.
- **qa-skeptic** — Assumes the work is broken and tries to break it against the spec. “The builder said the tests pass” is not proof; a command it ran and its output are. May write a failing test, never a fix.
- **owasp-hacker** — Attacks each story as a signed-in member: access, CSRF, injection, tokens. Local dev servers only, never a deployed host or real credentials. Proves a hole with a failing test, never a fix.
- **a11y-expert** — Checks every story against WCAG 2.2: keyboard, screen reader, zoom, motion. Reviews, never fixes. May write a failing axe or keyboard test.
- **pr-finalizer** — Runs every check, cuts readable commits, and writes the PR. The only agent that commits, and it asks before every push.
- **mentor** — Turns each finished story into a short lesson tied to its files. Checks every claim against the official docs. Never changes code.

I keep skills in the repo like code. They’re validated against the Agent Skills schema, audited for token cost and trigger collisions by analyzers I wrote, and third-party skills are pinned by content hash in a lockfile.

### Context is a budget

Context is a budget. When I measured my token usage, 93% was spent in sessions that had grown past 150k tokens, and 58% was Playwright MCP output left sitting in context. I restructured around that: a model tier per workflow step, instructions loaded only when a step runs, and compacting after every gate.

- **Sessions past 150k context** — 93% of tokens
- **Playwright MCP output** — 58% of tokens

I’m building an open-source AI toolkit around this, designed to stay coding-standards agnostic: a project points at its own standards repo when it initializes, so teams keep their conventions and still share one workflow. Agent behaviour lives in one provider-agnostic manifest and standards live in their own files, which is what makes that split possible.
